name: Half-Windsor knot

lead: The half-Windsor is a necktie knot that sits between small knots like the four-in-hand and the large full Windsor. It forms a symmetrical triangle with a central dimple, which makes a collar and tie look tidy and balanced.

It is the knot many people use for business and semi-formal dress because it suits most shirt collars and uses less tie length than a full Windsor. There is no research on it; the case for it is standard menswear practice.

paras: The knot is tied by hand in front of a mirror, with the wide end of the tie wrapped once around the narrow end and passed through the neck loop. Reference guides name it knot 7 in The 85 Ways to Tie a Tie, with a self-releasing variation also described. It works well with light and medium-weight fabrics, while thick ties tend to make a larger knot.

There are no health risks specific to the knot; a tie that is pulled too tight at the collar can be uncomfortable. Very thick ties or short ties can produce a knot that is bulky or leaves the tie too short.

angle.text: The half-Windsor lets someone present a tidy, symmetrical collar area with a standard-length tie. Its medium size suits most collar shapes and tie widths.

lead: The half-Windsor knot, also called the single Windsor, is a symmetrical necktie knot that is larger than the four-in-hand and Pratt knots but smaller than the full Windsor [1][2]. It forms a neat triangular shape and works well with light and medium-weight fabrics [2].

People use it to look polished at work, interviews and formal events. Menswear guides describe its even, symmetrical shape and a centered dimple as the feature that frames the collar uniformly [1]. It is a simplified form of the Windsor knot: the tie is brought around the loop on one side only, which makes it less bulky and shorter in fabric use [2].
Style sources link the knot's name to the Duke of Windsor's taste for wide knots [1]. No studies have examined the half-Windsor's effect on how people are perceived.

paras: The half-Windsor is a medium-sized symmetrical triangle. Grokipedia describes it as having a pronounced dimple and as suiting standard tie widths of roughly 2.5 to 3.5 inches [1]. It is a simplified Windsor in which the wide end wraps around the neck loop on one side only [2].
Using fewer passes than the full Windsor means it needs less tie length, so it suits ties of standard length [1].
Light and medium-weight fabrics work well [2]. Grokipedia says silk's smooth surface gives a clearer dimple while wool grips better but gives a subtler one [1].

The 85 Ways to Tie a Tie records the standard half-Windsor as 'Li Ro Ci Lo Ri Co T' and a self-releasing variation as 'Li Ro Ci Ro Li Co T' [2]. Menswear guides show the wide end being crossed, wrapped behind the narrow end and passed through the neck loop before the final pass through the front [1].

Reference sources give no firm history for the half-Windsor itself. Style writing connects its design to the broad knots associated with the Duke of Windsor in the early twentieth century, with the half-Windsor arising as a less bulky adaptation [1].
The knot is a common recommendation in general menswear guides for business and semi-formal dress because it balances size and ease [1].
